The series is a continuation of Meta’s “Scam se Bacho” educational campaign in collaboration with MIB, Prasar Bharati, SEBI, and I4C. The series premieres on Instagram and will soon be available on Waves OTT, streaming platform launched by Prasar Bharati. Meta has partnered with The Ministry of Information & Broadcasting (MIB), Prasar Bharati, Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), and Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) to launch India’s first government-led public interest microdrama series on online scams. The series will premiere on Instagram and will soon be available on Waves OTT. The “Scam se Bacho” microdrama will be Waves OTT’s inaugural series with Meta that aims to educate audiences on some of the most prevalent online scams today, including fake job offers , investment and digital arrest scams, reiterating the importance of reporting suspicious behaviour online and encouraging users to call the national cybercrime helpline 1930 in case of fraud. Through an engaging, social-first approach, this initiative builds on the growing popularity of microdramas and demonstrates how innovative storytelling formats can be harnessed to make important public interest information more accessible and relatable. Scam Se Bacho: Raising Awareness Through A Whole-Of-Society Approach Building on Meta’s flagship anti-scam campaign “Scam se Bacho” – this latest initiative expands our educational efforts and reinforces the importance of tackling online scams through a whole-of-society approach by bringing together government agencies, creators and industry partners to reach audiences through India’s fastest-growing storytelling format. “India’s creator economy is witnessing remarkable growth, with new storytelling formats opening up opportunities for creators across the country. Waves OTT and Prasar Bharati are committed to nurturing these emerging formats while ensuring they can also be used to serve the public interest with microdramas like Scam se Bacho. This partnership brings together government, industry and creators to demonstrate how compelling storytelling can educate, inform and empower citizens, while strengthening India’s leadership in the evolving digital content landscape.” – Shri Gaurav Dwivedi, CEO of Prasar Bharati “Financial fraud continues to evolve rapidly, making awareness and timely information critical for investor protection. Through SEBI’s ongoing Samajh Se Investing Simple campaign, we aim to simplify investing and promote informed financial decisions. By using an emerging content format like microdramas, this collaboration will help people understand complex fraud patterns and encourage them to verify information before making financial decisions. We believe public awareness initiatives such as Scam Se Bacho play an important role in building financially aware and empowered citizens.” – Shri Sanjay C Purao, Executive Director, Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) “We are witnessing a rise in cyber frauds, including ‘digital arrest’ scams where criminals pose as law enforcement officials to intimidate citizens. These scams often rely on fear and urgency to prevent victims from verifying information. Public awareness and timely reporting are critical to combating such crimes. Campaigns like Scam Se Bacho play an important role in educating people on identifying red flags and taking immediate action.” – Shri Nishant Kumar, Director, Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) “Awareness works best when people recognise scams and warning signs in situations that feel familiar to them. Building on three successful editions of our ‘Scam Se Bacho’ campaign with government partners, this mobile-first microdrama series takes scam education beyond films and advisories. With Meta’s continued investments in technology, safety tools and a whole-of-society approach in collaboration with the government, industry and creators, we hope to help millions pause, verify and report before a scam can succeed.” – Aman Jain, Senior Director & Head of Public Policy, Meta India As part of the series, Meta has also released a comic strip driving awareness around common scam types like Investment scams and Digital Arrest scams – alerting people to spot signs early, urging them to pause, question and verify information that seems suspicious and always relying on safety tools to help avoid digital fraud. Launched in 2024, Meta’s “Scam se Bacho” awareness campaign reached more than 400 million users in India across Facebook and Instagram in 2024–2025. Through celebrity-led campaigns featuring Ayushmann Khurrana and Neena Gupta, as well as partnerships with regional creators, the initiative aims to empower people to combat online scams. Ongoing Collaboration With I4C To Educate Older Adults Last Month, Meta collaborated with I4C and Saksham Senior to launch specialized educational campaigns designed to help senior citizens identify and protect themselves against evolving scam archetypes. Launched as part of I4C’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month initiatives, the campaign aims to empower vulnerable demographics by featuring them as confident protagonists who actively champion scam awareness within their families and communities as opposed to traditional narratives that portray older adults merely as victims. articles.title: Meta Welcomes Loblaw as First Canadian Retail Partner to Muse
articles.excerpt: Starting today, Loblaw is bringing its catalogue to Muse as a partner connector, the first Canadian retailer to do so. Connectors are a big reason Muse can do so much. Canadians can connect their Muse to apps they already use, including Gmail, Google Calendar and Instagram, so it can help them manage email, coordinate schedules and draw on saved content to get everyday tasks done. With participating Loblaw banners, Canadian shoppers can now ask Muse to help with meal planning, build their basket and check-out, all in Muse. Muse can remember brand preferences and information like food allergies, making next week’s planning even easier. Making this technology work for everyone requires careful design and engineering to operate more safely. Muse runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated computer in the cloud that securely stores the data and credentials for the services you connect, while keeping passwords and payment methods out of the agent’s view. You choose what your Muse can access, and it checks with you before sensitive actions such as sending an email or making a purchase. To learn more about how we built safety into Muse, this post explains our approach in detail. Talk It Through With Muse: Voice Now Available in Canada At Connect 2026, we previewed real-time conversations with your Muse. Two weeks ago, we introduced voice and now we’re rolling it out in Canada in the Muse app on mobile, web and on Mac — just tap the phone icon in the top-right corner to start talking. Sometimes it’s easier to think out loud. With voice, you can talk through an idea with your Muse and let it take shape without worrying about the exact prompt. As your Muse speaks, the avatar uses subtle expressions and gestures that match the tone of the conversation. It reacts while you talk, so you can tell it’s following along. And you choose how present you want it to be: voice only, the avatar alongside your conversation, or full screen when you want to talk face to face. A space is a custom experience you create inside Muse by describing your idea, like a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, or a planning board for your next DIY project. It’s shaped around your routines, goals, and interests, and can be as practical or entertaining as you want. articles.title: An Update on the Content We Recommend on Instagram in India
articles.excerpt: We've strengthened the default protections behind what Instagram recommends in India to reduce unwanted content and improve people’s experience on Instagram. This work has been guided by what our users told us they want from their recommendations. The post An Update on the Content We Recommend on Instagram in India appeared first on Meta Newsroom .

This work has been guided by what our users told us they want from their recommendations. Today, we’re sharing an update on this work. How Recommendations Work At Instagram, we make personalized recommendations to help people discover new communities and content. Our goal is to make recommendations that are relevant and valuable to each person who sees them. For example, if you interact with restaurants and bookstores on Instagram, we may recommend content about food, recipes, books, or reading. Recommendations include content from accounts you don’t already follow, in places like Explore, Reels and Feed , so we apply guidelines specific to them. Through our Recommendations Guidelines , we work to avoid recommending content that could be low quality, objectionable or particularly sensitive. We use technology to detect content and accounts that don’t meet those guidelines and to help us avoid recommending them. As always, content that goes against our Community Standards is removed from Instagram, and content that is unlawful in a country is restricted there. What We’ve Changed Better detection: Around the world, our systems check content against our Recommendations Guidelines before we recommend it. We’ve been improving those systems, including using more capable AI models that assess content directly rather than waiting for someone to report or hide it, so we catch more of what people don’t want to see. Tuned for India: We’ve improved our systems specifically for India so they catch more of what people here told us they didn’t want to see. Today, our systems keep more of this content out of recommendations, including sexually suggestive content and content that depicts violence. Since these changes, we’ve been able to proactively reduce more content in India that doesn’t meet our Recommendations Guidelines. As a result, we’ve seen people report recommended content about half as often as they were a year ago. Your feedback shapes this too. When someone hides a post or taps “Not interested,” that tells us what not to recommend to them, and helps us understand what people don’t want to see. Controls Over What You See and Who Can Reach You Alongside the standards we apply for everyone, you have controls to adjust what you see and who can reach you: Sensitive Content Control lets people choose to see less sensitive content in their recommendations, across Search, Reels, Explore, suggested accounts, and in-Feed recommendations. It’s in Settings and Activity, under Content Preferences. In India, the most mature content isn’t recommended, so this control adjusts what you see within that. Political Content Control lets people choose to see less political content in recommendations from accounts they don’t follow. It’s in Settings and Activity, under Content Preferences → Political Content. Not Interested lets people tell us a recommendation isn’t for them, by tapping the three dots on a post or reel. Hidden Words filters chosen words, phrases, and emojis out of comments and message requests. Block prevents someone from finding a profile, seeing posts, or sending messages, and also covers new accounts they try to create. Teens have additional age appropriate protections. Last year, we introduced Teen Accounts in India, which automatically places teens in a 13+ content setting shaped by our age-appropriate content guidelines . Our Continued Work We’re committed to improving our systems as user behavior and technology changes, and we’ll keep listening to what people in India tell us they want to see. We publish data on how we enforce our policies in our global Community Standards Enforcement Report , and in the monthly transparency report we publish for India under the IT Rules, 2021.
